newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds mixed in moderate trade on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds mixed in moderate trade on U.S. data.

text.p: Irish bonds were mixed in moderate trade on Thursday, edging out of negative territory on the back of market-supportive U.S. payroll figures, dealers said.

"The payroll data have given all bond markets a bit of a boost," one dealer said. "The Irish market is being further underpinned by yesterday's mid-year EBR figures which point to the possibility of a balanced budget."
However, Irish bonds continued to underperform German Bunds by several basis points, he added.
The June employment report out of the U.S. showed an overall increase in payrolls of 217,000 - under expectations - and the private sector number was up by just 151,000.
By 1520 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down three pence at 102.82 to yield 5.73 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 15 pence at 110.90 to yield 6.38 percent.
Irish bond yields against Bunds widened slightly from Wednesday's close to 150 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 90 over in the 10-year.
Dealers said Wednesday's UK Budget was within market expectations and would have little impact on the Irish market.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on Wednesday raised around six billion pounds in new taxes.

But with around 90 percent of the tax rises directed at the corporate sector, the remaining 10 percent, or 750 million stg, aimed at households was widely seen as insufficient to dampen rampant domestic demand.
Many analysts believe the Bank of England will have little choice but to raise interest rates when it meets next week.
The Irish pound and rumours of its revaluation - despite its unlikelihood in the short term - continued to be supportive in the market, dealers said.
If sterling passed the three mark level, however, it could pose difficulties for the punt, a dealer said.
"The further the punt falls against sterling the greater the inflation risk and the more uncertainty in the market."
Yesterday's statement by the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) had been received by the bond market as "something of a damp squib" dealers said.
"We think the EBR number was too conservative," a dealer said. "So the NTMA could have reduced the gross bond supply figure by a further few hundred million pounds."
The NTMA said on Wednesday that it had reduced its funding requirement from 2.6 billion Irish pounds to 2.4 billion.
Yesterday's mid-year Exchequer Returns showed as a higher-than-expected surplus of 721 million pounds.
